claim: Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a chronic and debilitating neglected tropical disease caused by the filarial nematodes Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori.
source: Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a chronic and debilitating neglected tropical disease caused by the filarial nematodes Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about the causative agents of lymphatic filariasis.

claim: Infective-stage larvae are transmitted by mosquitoes to the human definitive host, where they develop and molt to adult stages that persist in the lymphatics and produce blood-circulating pre-larval stage microfilariae (mf).
source: Infective-stage larvae are transmitted by mosquitoes to the human definitive host, where they develop and molt to adult stages that persist in the lymphatics and produce blood-circulating pre-larval stage microfilariae (mf) (Roberts et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2009, describing the life cycle of filarial nematodes.

claim: LF afflicts an estimated 51 million individuals in tropical and subtropical climates around the world.
source: LF afflicts an estimated 51 million individuals in tropical and subtropical climates around the world and endangers nearly a billion individuals worldwide (Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators, 2020; Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators, 2020; World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological data from the Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators and the World Health Organization.

claim: LF endangers nearly a billion individuals worldwide.
source: LF afflicts an estimated 51 million individuals in tropical and subtropical climates around the world and endangers nearly a billion individuals worldwide (Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators, 2020; Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators, 2020; World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological data from the Local Burden of Disease 2019 Neglected Tropical Diseases Collaborators and the World Health Organization.

claim: Chronic cases of LF manifest in elephantiasis, an extreme buildup of lymph resulting in stigmatizing disfiguration and additional socioeconomic challenges.
source: Chronic cases of LF manifest in elephantiasis, an extreme buildup of lymph resulting in stigmatizing disfiguration and additional socioeconomic challenges (Ton et al., 2015; Weiss, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ton et al., 2015 and Weiss, 2008, describing the clinical manifestations and social impacts of chronic LF.

claim: Mass drug administration (MDA) in endemic settings with combinations of ivermectin (IVM), diethylcarbamazine (DEC), and albendazole (ABZ) is used to disrupt parasite transmission, but this approach is only effective with years of repeated treatment.
source: Mass drug administration (MDA) in endemic settings with combinations of ivermectin (IVM), diethylcarbamazine (DEC), and albendazole (ABZ) is used to disrupt parasite transmission, but this approach is only effective with years of repeated treatment.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about current treatment strategies for LF and their limitations.

claim: Contraindications for antifilarial drugs exist in regions co-endemic for other filarial parasites.
source: Additionally, contraindications for antifilarial drugs exist in regions co-endemic for other filarial parasites (Chippaux et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chippaux et al., 1996, describing contraindications for antifilarial drugs in co-endemic regions.

claim: There is a growing threat of resistance to anthelmintics.
source: With no cure and the growing threat of resistance to anthelmintics (Campbell, 1982; Geary et al., 2011; Geary et al., 2010; Ismail et al., 1999; Osei-Atweneboana et al., 2011; Wolstenholme et al., 2015), there is a clear need to improve our understanding of basic biological processes that underpin the host–parasite interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting anthelmintic resistance.

claim: The excretory-secretory (ES) products of parasitic nematodes are known to be essential for parasite survival within the host.
source: The excretory-secretory (ES) products of parasitic nematodes are known to be essential for parasite survival within the host (Harnett, 2014; Hotterbeekx et al., 2021; Lightowlers and Rickard, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harnett, 2014; Hotterbeekx et al., 2021; and Lightowlers and Rickard, 1988.

claim: The ES system is a conduit for the release of immunomodulatory proteins and extracellular vesicles that promote parasite survival.
source: Despite the general understanding that the ES system is a conduit for the release of immunomodulatory proteins and extracellular vesicles that promote parasite survival, the biology of the ES system has yet to be investigated in medically important parasitic nematodes.
evidence: This is described as a 'general understanding' in the field, indicating established knowledge.

claim: The biology of the ES system has yet to be investigated in medically important parasitic nematodes.
source: Despite the general understanding that the ES system is a conduit for the release of immunomodulatory proteins and extracellular vesicles that promote parasite survival, the biology of the ES system has yet to be investigated in medically important parasitic nematodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Profiling of secretions across the filarial nematode life cycle has helped identify antigens that have been pursued therapeutically and diagnostically.
source: Profiling of secretions (Bennuru et al., 2011; Harischandra et al., 2018; Hewitson et al., 2008; Kaushal et al., 1982; Moreno and Geary, 2008; Zamanian et al., 2015) across the filarial nematode life cycle has helped identify antigens that have been pursued therapeutically and diagnostically (Harnett, 2014; Kalyanasundaram et al., 2020; Maizels et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2013), but the origins of these proteins and the tissue systems that underlie their release at the host–parasite interface are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting secretion profiling and antigen identification studies.

claim: The origins of secreted proteins and the tissue systems that underlie their release at the host–parasite interface are unknown.
source: Profiling of secretions (Bennuru et al., 2011; Harischandra et al., 2018; Hewitson et al., 2008; Kaushal et al., 1982; Moreno and Geary, 2008; Zamanian et al., 2015) across the filarial nematode life cycle has helped identify antigens that have been pursued therapeutically and diagnostically (Harnett, 2014; Kalyanasundaram et al., 2020; Maizels et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2013), but the origins of these proteins and the tissue systems that underlie their release at the host–parasite interface are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Recent studies have implicated secretory processes as a target of existing anthelmintics.
source: Recent studies have also implicated secretory processes as a target of existing anthelmintics (Moreno et al., 2021; Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moreno et al., 2021 and Moreno et al., 2010.

claim: IVM causes rapid clearance of mf from host blood at concentrations that do not cause overt fitness effects on cultured parasites.
source: IVM causes rapid clearance of mf from host blood at concentrations that do not cause overt fitness effects on cultured parasites.
evidence: This is a statement of observed phenomena in the field.

claim: IVM unmasks mf from the host immune system by inhibiting protein and vesicle secretion.
source: This disconnect is reconciled by a model whereby IVM unmasks mf from the host immune system by inhibiting protein and vesicle secretion (Rao et al., 1987; Vatta et al., 2014; Zahner et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rao et al., 1987; Vatta et al., 2014; and Zahner et al., 1997.

claim: The ES apparatus is thought to be the primary source of immunogenic proteins in the mf stage.
source: While the ES apparatus is thought to be the primary source of immunogenic proteins in the mf stage, the cells that comprise this structure and control secretion have not been characterized.
evidence: This is described as a prevailing thought in the field.

claim: The cells that comprise the ES apparatus and control secretion have not been characterized.
source: While the ES apparatus is thought to be the primary source of immunogenic proteins in the mf stage, the cells that comprise this structure and control secretion have not been characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Clear morphological descriptions of the filarial ES system are currently restricted to the mf stage.
source: Clear morphological descriptions of the filarial ES system are currently restricted to the mf stage, but microscopy studies confirm that this structure is present in L3 and adult parasites (Airs et al., 2022; Landmann et al., 2010; Mutafchiev et al., 2014; Tongu, 1974).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge, with citations supporting the presence of the structure in other stages.

claim: The ES structure is present in L3 and adult parasites.
source: Clear morphological descriptions of the filarial ES system are currently restricted to the mf stage, but microscopy studies confirm that this structure is present in L3 and adult parasites (Airs et al., 2022; Landmann et al., 2010; Mutafchiev et al., 2014; Tongu, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to microscopy studies.

claim: Filarial parasites possess tubular ES systems featuring a single large excretory cell connected through a cytoplasmic bridge to an excretory vesicle and pore.
source: Filarial parasites possess tubular ES systems featuring a single large excretory cell connected through a cytoplasmic bridge to an excretory vesicle and pore (Tongu, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tongu, 1974.

claim: In C. elegans, the ES system is a well-studied and critical osmoregulatory and excretory organ made up of a pore cell, duct cell, excretory/canal cell, and canal-associated neurons (CAN).
source: In the free-living model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, the ES system is a well-studied and critical osmoregulatory and excretory organ made up of a pore cell, duct cell, excretory/canal cell, and canal-associated neurons (CAN) (Sundaram and Buechner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sundaram and Buechner, 2016.

claim: There is significant diversification of ES anatomy and function between C. elegans and filariae and more generally across nematode clades.
source: However, significant diversification of ES anatomy and function between C. elegans and filariae and more generally across nematode clades (A. F. Bird, 1991) demands more species-specific approaches to the study of ES systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to A. F. Bird, 1991.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics has facilitated resolution of cellular processes and functions that are masked in tissue level or bulk transcriptomic approaches.
source: Single-cell transcriptomics has facilitated resolution of cellular processes and functions that are masked in tissue level or bulk transcriptomic approaches.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the capabilities of single-cell transcriptomics.

claim: Single-cell suspensions generated from tissue dispersions of free-living nematodes have enabled high-dimensional transcriptomic analysis of cell types across developmental stages.
source: Single-cell suspensions generated from tissue dispersions of free-living nematodes (Zhang et al., 2011) have enabled high-dimensional transcriptomic analysis of cell types across developmental stages (Ben-David et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2017; Packer et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2011) and provide a pathway to the characterization of essential cells and tissues in related parasites, including those that control secretory behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting single-cell studies in free-living nematodes.

claim: Viable cell suspensions have yet to be leveraged to transcriptomically profile human, animal, or plant parasitic nematodes at single-cell resolution.
source: However, viable cell suspensions have yet to be leveraged to transcriptomically profile human, animal, or plant parasitic nematodes at single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: We applied single-cell approaches to generate and annotate a cell atlas of gene expression in B. malayi microfilariae.
source: Here, we applied single-cell approaches to generate and annotate a cell atlas of gene expression in B. malayi microfilariae and to map secretory-associated cell types and the distributions of prominent antigens and anthelmintic targets.
evidence: This is a statement of the work performed in this study.

claim: We mapped secretory-associated cell types and the distributions of prominent antigens and anthelmintic targets.
source: Here, we applied single-cell approaches to generate and annotate a cell atlas of gene expression in B. malayi microfilariae and to map secretory-associated cell types and the distributions of prominent antigens and anthelmintic targets.
evidence: This is a statement of the work performed in this study.

claim: We evaluated the effects of anthelmintics on parasite cells and the amenability of mf cell suspensions to longer-term culture.
source: We evaluated the effects of anthelmintics on parasite cells and the amenability of mf cell suspensions to longer-term culture.
evidence: This is a statement of the work performed in this study.

claim: Prominent antigens are transcriptionally derived from both secretory and non-secretory cell and tissue types.
source: We show that prominent antigens are transcriptionally derived from both secretory and non-secretory cell and tissue types, and anthelmintic targets display distinct expression patterns across neuronal, muscular, and other cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the single-cell transcriptomic data.

claim: Anthelmintic targets display distinct expression patterns across neuronal, muscular, and other cell types.
source: We show that prominent antigens are transcriptionally derived from both secretory and non-secretory cell and tissue types, and anthelmintic targets display distinct expression patterns across neuronal, muscular, and other cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on the single-cell transcriptomic data.

claim: The major classes of anthelmintics do not affect the viability of isolated cells at pharmacological concentrations.
source: While the major classes of anthelmintics do not affect the viability of isolated cells at pharmacological concentrations, we observe cell-specific transcriptional shifts in response to ivermectin.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on drug treatment experiments on isolated cells.

claim: We observe cell-specific transcriptional shifts in response to ivermectin.
source: While the major classes of anthelmintics do not affect the viability of isolated cells at pharmacological concentrations, we observe cell-specific transcriptional shifts in response to ivermectin.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on single-cell RNA-seq of drug-treated cells.

claim: We introduce a microfilariae cell culture model to enable future functional studies of parasitic nematode cells.
source: Finally, we introduce a microfilariae cell culture model to enable future functional studies of parasitic nematode cells.
evidence: This is a statement of a method developed in this study.

claim: These methods are expected to be readily adaptable to other parasitic nematode species and stages.
source: We expect these methods to be readily adaptable to other parasitic nematode species and stages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applicability of the methods.

claim: B. malayi mf are small (~177–230 µm in length, ~5–7 µm in diameter).
source: This pre-larval life stage is small (~177–230 µm in length, ~5–7 µm in diameter) but can be isolated from peritoneal fluid of infected jirds in large quantities (millions), potentially facilitating insight into early parasite development and the capture of rare cell types.
evidence: This is a statement of known morphological characteristics of B. malayi mf.

claim: B. malayi mf can be isolated from peritoneal fluid of infected jirds in large quantities (millions).
source: This pre-larval life stage is small (~177–230 µm in length, ~5–7 µm in diameter) but can be isolated from peritoneal fluid of infected jirds in large quantities (millions), potentially facilitating insight into early parasite development and the capture of rare cell types.
evidence: This is a statement of established methods for obtaining B. malayi mf.

claim: Microfilariae suspensions recovered from the jird peritoneal cavity are developmentally asynchronous and include an abundance of host cells, tissue debris, embryos, and nonviable mf.
source: Microfilariae suspensions recovered from the jird peritoneal cavity are developmentally asynchronous and include an abundance of host cells, tissue debris, embryos, and nonviable mf, all of which contribute to transcriptomic contamination.
evidence: This is an observation from the study about the composition of peritoneal lavages.

claim: PD-10 desalting columns reliably recovered high yields (60–70%) of highly motile mf.
source: This method reliably recovered high yields (60–70%) of highly motile mf that were then used as input into tissue dispersion reactions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study about the efficiency of the PD-10 filtration method.

claim: B. malayi mf are encapsulated within an impermeable eggshell of carbohydrates including chitin.
source: B. malayi mf are encapsulated within an impermeable eggshell of carbohydrates including chitin (Fuhrman and Piessens, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fuhrman and Piessens, 1985.

claim: Chitinase treatment did not cause complete exsheathment, but produced a visible shrinking effect in the tail and head spaces indicating sheath breach.
source: Chitinase treatment did not cause complete exsheathment, but produced a visible shrinking effect in the tail and head spaces indicating sheath breach (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on microscopy of chitinase-treated mf, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: SDS-DTT treatment effectively compromised cuticular structure and inhibited motility without causing parasite death.
source: Incubation in diluted SDS-DTT effectively compromised cuticular structure and inhibited motility without causing parasite death (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on experiments with SDS-DTT treatment, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: mf cuticles were visibly compromised after approximately 20 min of pronase digestion.
source: mf cuticles were visibly compromised after approximately 20 min of digestion, where the midsection of the filarial body plan exhibits protrusions that break and release cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the study based on monitoring pronase digestion.

claim: A total of 20,000 objects were assessed by imaging flow cytometry.
source: A total of 20,000 objects were assessed and 15,683 were identified as debris, undigested worm segments, or nonviable cells as indicated by negative Calcein-AM staining, a cell-permeable viability dye that remains within healthy cells after acetoxymethyl (AM) cleavage by non-specific esterase activity.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental procedure and results from imaging flow cytometry.

claim: 15,683 objects were identified as debris, undigested worm segments, or nonviable cells.
source: A total of 20,000 objects were assessed and 15,683 were identified as debris, undigested worm segments, or nonviable cells as indicated by negative Calcein-AM staining, a cell-permeable viability dye that remains within healthy cells after acetoxymethyl (AM) cleavage by non-specific esterase activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging flow cytometry analysis.

claim: 2893 objects were identified as live, single cells that displayed round cellular and nuclear morphology.
source: The remaining 4317 objects were analyzed using post-acquisition image features to identify 2893 objects as live, single cells that displayed round cellular and nuclear morphology (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging flow cytometry analysis, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The majority of recovered cells have a diameter of 5.23 ± 0.77 µm.
source: While the majority of recovered cells have a diameter of 5.23 ± 0.77 µm, each mf is known to possess a large and morphologically distinct secretory cell that is critical to parasite survival and immune evasion in the host (Tongu, 1974; Hewitson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a measurement from the imaging flow cytometry data.

claim: Each mf possesses a large and morphologically distinct secretory cell that is critical to parasite survival and immune evasion in the host.
source: While the majority of recovered cells have a diameter of 5.23 ± 0.77 µm, each mf is known to possess a large and morphologically distinct secretory cell that is critical to parasite survival and immune evasion in the host (Tongu, 1974; Hewitson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tongu, 1974 and Hewitson et al., 2008.

claim: The Brugia secretory cell is hypothesized to be responsible for the release of prominent antigens, extracellular vesicles, and nucleic acids that operate at the host-parasite interface.
source: The Brugia secretory cell is hypothesized to be responsible for the release of prominent antigens, extracellular vesicles, and nucleic acids that operate at the host-parasite interface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the manuscript.

claim: Classical descriptions of the mf ES system highlight the secretory cell as a large cell with bipolar canal extensions.
source: Classical descriptions of the mf ES system highlight the secretory cell as a large cell with bipolar canal extensions (Moreno et al., 2010; Nelson and Riddle, 1984; Sundaram and Buechner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical descriptions of the ES system.

claim: A total of 11 cells with bipolar appendages were identified, which are notably the largest identifiable cells (8.46 ± 0.77 µm in diameter) in the mf stage.
source: We mined cells in our dataset that match this description and identified a total of 11 cells with bipolar appendages that are notably the largest identifiable cells (8.46 ± 0.77 µm in diameter) in this life stage (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging flow cytometry analysis, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Each mf possesses a single secretory cell among hundreds of total cells.
source: Each mf possesses a single secretory cell among hundreds of total cells, and this recovery rate (0.4%) falls within the expected range, providing us confidence that our dispersion protocol captures both common and rare cell types.
evidence: This is a statement of known anatomy of mf.

claim: The recovery rate of secretory cells (0.4%) falls within the expected range.
source: Each mf possesses a single secretory cell among hundreds of total cells, and this recovery rate (0.4%) falls within the expected range, providing us confidence that our dispersion protocol captures both common and rare cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and the observed recovery rate.

claim: Dimensional reduction of 46,621 filtered cells via UMAP identified 27 transcriptionally distinct clusters.
source: Dimensional reduction of 46,621 filtered cells via Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (McInnes et al., 2018) identified 27 transcriptionally distinct clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: A median of 230 genes and 267 reads per cell were achieved across all cells in the dataset.
source: Across all cells in the dataset, a median of 230 genes and 267 reads per cell were achieved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quality metric from the single-cell RNA-seq data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transcript abundance of single cells strongly correlated with microfilariae bulk gene expression (r = 0.85, R2 = 0.72, p=2.2 × 10–16).
source: Transcript abundance of single cells strongly correlated with microfilariae bulk gene expression (Reaves et al., 2018; Figure 2A, inset, r = 0.85, R2 = 0.72, p=2.2 × 10–16), providing additional evidence that our single-cell pipeline largely recapitulates the cell-type distribution and transcriptional profile of the intact parasite.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data, with reference to Figure 2A inset.

claim: The single-cell pipeline largely recapitulates the cell-type distribution and transcriptional profile of the intact parasite.
source: Transcript abundance of single cells strongly correlated with microfilariae bulk gene expression (Reaves et al., 2018; Figure 2A, inset, r = 0.85, R2 = 0.72, p=2.2 × 10–16), providing additional evidence that our single-cell pipeline largely recapitulates the cell-type distribution and transcriptional profile of the intact parasite.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong correlation between single-cell and bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: B. malayi transcription factors show both specific and broad-based activity that aligns with known C. elegans patterns.
source: An analysis of B. malayi transcription factors shows both specific and broad-based transcription factor activity that aligns with known C. elegans patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: lin-14 exhibits broad expression in the B. malayi mf scRNA-seq data and is congruent with broad expression of the transcription factor in C. elegans.
source: For example, lin-14 exhibits broad expression in the B. malayi mf scRNA-seq data and is congruent with broad expression of the transcription factor in C. elegans (Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcription factor analysis, with a citation to C. elegans data.

claim: C. elegans has multiple cell-type-restricted transcription factors including ciliated sensory neuron transcription factor Cel-daf-19 and body wall muscle-specific transcription factors Cel-hlh-1 and Cel-unc-120.
source: In contrast, C. elegans has multiple cell-type-restricted transcription factors including ciliated sensory neuron transcription factor Cel-daf-19 and body wall muscle-specific transcription factors Cel-hlh-1 and Cel-unc-120 (Taylor et al., 2021), both of which show restricted cluster expression in the B. malayi mf scRNA-seq atlas.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2021.

claim: Cel-daf-19, Cel-hlh-1, and Cel-unc-120 show restricted cluster expression in the B. malayi mf scRNA-seq atlas.
source: In contrast, C. elegans has multiple cell-type-restricted transcription factors including ciliated sensory neuron transcription factor Cel-daf-19 and body wall muscle-specific transcription factors Cel-hlh-1 and Cel-unc-120 (Taylor et al., 2021), both of which show restricted cluster expression in the B. malayi mf scRNA-seq atlas.
evidence: This is a finding from the B. malayi transcription factor analysis.

claim: 16 UMAP clusters were annotated using markers for well-characterized C. elegans cell types with one-to-one B. malayi orthologs.
source: Markers for well-characterized C. elegans cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) with one-to-one B. malayi orthologs were used to annotate 16 UMAP clusters (Figure 2A), and pseudobulk analysis confirms the robustness of these markers for differentiating cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statement of the annotation approach and results, with references to figures.

claim: 18,317 cells (39.3% of global count) were assigned a cell-type annotation.
source: In total 18,317 cells (39.3% of global count) were assigned a cell-type annotation.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: 6,223 cells were identified as muscle derived (13.3% of global count).
source: Among these, 6,223 cells were identified as muscle derived (13.3% of global count) and 5,527 cells expressed pan-neuronal markers (11.9% of global count).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: 5,527 cells expressed pan-neuronal markers (11.9% of global count).
source: Among these, 6,223 cells were identified as muscle derived (13.3% of global count) and 5,527 cells expressed pan-neuronal markers (11.9% of global count).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: Cell types belonging to the mesoderm lineage include 10,284 cells (22% of global count).
source: Cell types belonging to the mesoderm lineage include 10,284 cells (22% of global count).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: Body wall muscle cells represent the majority of the mesodermal cells identified (clusters 2 and 19).
source: Body wall muscle cells represent the majority of the mesodermal cells identified (clusters 2 and 19) and are distinctly categorized based on expression of Bma-hlh-1 (Krause et al., 1994) and markers shown to be enriched in B. malayi body wall muscle such as actin and multiple myosins (Bma-myo-3, Bma-unc-54.1, Bma-unc-54.2, Bma-act-1) (Morris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell annotation analysis, with citations supporting the marker genes.

claim: Cluster 6 was annotated as coelomocytes using C. elegans orthologs (Bma-cup-4, Bm6921, Bma-unc-122, Bma-let-381).
source: Also belonging to the mesodermal cell lineage in C. elegans are coelomocytes, phagocytic scavengers located within the pseudocoel. Using coelomocyte-specific C. elegans orthologs (Bma-cup-4, Bm6921, Bma-unc-122, Bma-let-381), cluster 6 was annotated as coelomocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: Mesodermal cells in the post-embryonic and pre-larval mf state include well-differentiated body wall musculature and coelomocytes and underdeveloped enteric and vulval muscle structures.
source: These data show that mesodermal cells in the post-embryonic and pre-larval mf state include well-differentiated body wall musculature and coelomocytes and underdeveloped enteric and vulval muscle structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell annotation results.

claim: Pan-neuronal C. elegans markers (sbt-1, ric-4, ida-1, egl-3, egl-21) were used to identify nine clusters of putative neurons.
source: Pan-neuronal C. elegans markers (sbt-1, ric-4, ida-1, egl-3, egl-21) were used to identify nine clusters of putative neurons expressing all five markers (303 genes and 358 reads per cell) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement of the annotation approach for neurons, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Cluster 11 was identified as motor neurons characterized by the C. elegans motor neuron marker (Cel-unc-4).
source: We were able to further resolve a cluster of motor neurons (cluster 11) and interneurons (cluster 23) characterized by one-to-one orthologs of the C. elegans motor neuron marker (Cel-unc-4) and DVA tail interneuron marker (Cel-nlp-12), respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal cell annotation analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cluster 23 was identified as interneurons characterized by the DVA tail interneuron marker (Cel-nlp-12).
source: We were able to further resolve a cluster of motor neurons (cluster 11) and interneurons (cluster 23) characterized by one-to-one orthologs of the C. elegans motor neuron marker (Cel-unc-4) and DVA tail interneuron marker (Cel-nlp-12), respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal cell annotation analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Clusters 13 and 27 express Bma-daf-19 and genes involved in ciliogenesis and have been annotated as ciliated sensory neurons.
source: Clusters 13 and 27 express Bma-daf-19, an ortholog of the RFX-family transcription factor Cel-daf-19 shown to be directly responsible for cilia development in ciliated sensory neurons as well as genes involved in ciliogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Blacque et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2006; Narasimhan et al., 2015; Swoboda et al., 2000). These two clusters have been annotated as ciliated sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal cell annotation analysis, with citations supporting the marker genes and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Known genes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis and transport were used to map neuropeptidergic (cluster 26) and aminergic neurons (clusters 24 and 25).
source: Known genes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis and transport were used to map neuropeptidergic (cluster 26) and aminergic neurons (clusters 24 and 25) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement of the annotation approach for neurotransmitter-specific neurons, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The motor and interneuron neuronal clusters (11 and 23) express Bma-cha-1 and Bma-cho-1 in 10–15% of all captured cells.
source: The motor and interneuron neuronal clusters (11 and 23) express Bma-cha-1 and Bma-cho-1 in 10–15% of all captured cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the neurotransmitter analysis.

claim: Clusters 3–5 exhibit more abundant expression of Bma-cha-1 but no other neuronal markers and may represent a cholinergic neuronal developmental state.
source: Clusters 3–5 exhibit more abundant expression of Bma-cha-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) but no other neuronal markers, cholinergic or pan-neuronal, and may represent a cholinergic neuronal developmental state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the expression pattern in clusters 3–5, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The phylogenetic distance between free-living clade V C. elegans and filarial clade III nematodes is associated with known differences in anatomy and localization of some orthologous proteins.
source: The phylogenetic distance between free-living clade V C. elegans and filarial clade III nematodes is associated with known differences in anatomy (Chitwood and Chitwood, 1950) and localization of some orthologous proteins (Moreno et al., 2010), which limits efforts to comprehensively map all cell types across species (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and protein localization studies, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cluster 22 uniquely displays high expression of chitinases (Bma-cht-1.1, Bma-cht-1.2, Bma-cht-1.3) and the immunomodulatory vaccine candidates Bma-val-1 and Bm97.
source: A cluster of 503 cells (cluster 22) uniquely displays high expression of chitinases (Bma-cht-1.1, Bma-cht-1.2, Bma-cht-1.3) and the immunomodulatory vaccine candidates Bma-val-1 and Bm97.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster characterization analysis.

claim: Chitinase has been shown to be stored in the inner body of microfilariae that is positioned between the excretory and G1 cells and is hypothesized to act as the precursor for the intestinal tract of the developing larvae in the mosquito.
source: Chitinase has been shown to be stored in the inner body of microfilariae that is positioned between the excretory and G1 cells and is hypothesized to act as the precursor for the intestinal tract of the developing larvae in the mosquito (McLaren, 1972; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLaren, 1972 and Wu et al., 2008.

claim: Cluster 22 is annotated as inner body-associated cells based on the combination of chitinase and molting proteins.
source: The combination of chitinase and molting proteins within this segregated cluster supports the annotation of cluster 22 as inner body-associated cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and known biology of the inner body.

claim: B. malayi orthologs (Bma-pks-1, Bma-acbp-6, Bma-ceh-10) of CAN markers identify cluster 14 as ES CAN cells (1006 total cells).
source: B. malayi orthologs (Bma-pks-1, Bma-acbp-6, Bma-ceh-10) of CAN markers identify cluster 14 as ES CAN cells (1006 total cells).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell annotation analysis.

claim: The largest viable cells within a B. malayi microfilariae suspension were FAC-sorted and pooled for downstream RNA-seq.
source: We exploited the large size of the B. malayi secretory cell as a means to enrich for and profile this rare cell type within single-cell suspensions. The largest viable cells within a B. malayi microfilariae suspension were FAC-sorted and pooled for downstream RNA-seq (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental approach, with references to figures.

claim: Cluster 15 shows a clear overall enrichment for the 78 genes more highly expressed in the sorted 'Largest' cell population.
source: Cluster 15 shows a clear overall enrichment for the 78 genes more highly expressed in this sorted cell population (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1), and individual cells within this putative secretory cell cluster represent the largest group coexpressing different subsets of these markers (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the FACS-enriched cell analysis, with references to figures and source data.

claim: Individual cells within cluster 15 represent the largest group coexpressing different subsets of the 'Largest' cell markers.
source: Cluster 15 shows a clear overall enrichment for the 78 genes more highly expressed in this sorted cell population (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1), and individual cells within this putative secretory cell cluster represent the largest group coexpressing different subsets of these markers (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the coexpression analysis, with references to figures and source data.

claim: C. elegans excretory cell markers identified through FACS and RNA-seq lack clear orthologs or display no meaningful overlap with highly or uniquely expressed orthologous markers found in the B. malayi secretory cell.
source: Established and new C. elegans excretory cell markers identified through this effort lack clear orthologs or display no meaningful overlap with highly or uniquely expressed orthologous markers found in the B. malayi secretory cell.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing C. elegans and B. malayi excretory cell markers.

claim: The lack of overlap between C. elegans and B. malayi excretory cell markers aligns with the distinct evolutionary history of the ES system in filariae and the parasite-specific functions the secretory cell is likely to perform in the host context.
source: This aligns with the distinct evolutionary history of the ES system in filariae and the parasite-specific functions the secretory cell is likely to perform in the host context.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lack of marker overlap and known evolutionary divergence.

claim: Transcripts encoding for secreted proteins exhibit variable patterns of expression across the body and very few are specifically localized to the secretory cell (cluster 15).
source: Transcripts encoding for secreted proteins exhibit variable patterns of expression across the body and very few are specifically localized to the secretory cell (cluster 15).
evidence: This is a finding from mapping secreted protein transcripts to cell types.

claim: Some prominent antigens that are expressed across many tissue types (Bma-tpi-1 and Bma-cpi-2) have been localized to the ES apparatus via whole-mount antibody staining.
source: Some prominent antigens that are expressed across many tissue types (Bma-tpi-1 and Bma-cpi-2) have been localized to the ES apparatus via whole-mount antibody staining (Moreno et al., 2010), an observation that is likely reconciled by aggregation and secretion of these proteins through the ES apparatus.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moreno et al., 2010, with an inference about protein aggregation and secretion.

claim: Broadly expressed antigens that are included as vaccine targets and diagnostic markers include Bma-tpi-1, Bma-sxp-2, and Bm3837.
source: Additional broadly expressed antigens that are included as vaccine targets and diagnostic markers include Bma-tpi-1, Bma-sxp-2, and Bm3837 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Krushna et al., 2009; Lalitha et al., 2002; Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the antigen expression analysis, with citations and references to figures.

claim: Bma-val-1, Bm97, and chitinases (Bma-cht-1.1 and Bma-cht-1.2) have strong and nearly undivided expression in the inner body.
source: Bma-val-1, Bm97, and chitinases (Bma-cht-1.1 and Bma-cht-1.2) have strong and nearly undivided expression in the inner body (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the antigen expression analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Notable genes that showed strong or exclusive expression in the annotated secretory cells include microfilariae-specific serpin Bma-srp-2 and diagnostic antigens Bm10631 (BmR1) and Bm14.
source: Notable genes that showed strong or exclusive expression in the annotated secretory cells include microfilariae-specific serpin Bma-srp-2 and diagnostic antigens Bm10631 (BmR1) (Greene et al., 2022) and Bm14, a Cys2His2 zinc finger (C2H2-ZF) transcription factor (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the secretory cell expression analysis, with a citation and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: A greater fraction of proteins with transcripts enriched in the secretory cell contain signal peptides (43%) compared to other cell types.
source: A greater fraction of proteins with transcripts enriched in the secretory cell contain signal peptides (43%) compared to other cell types (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the signal peptide analysis, with reference to Figure 4A and source data.

claim: 41.8% of proteins with transcripts enriched in the secretory cell are predicted to contain transmembrane domains.
source: 41.8% of proteins with transcripts enriched in the secretory cell are predicted to contain transmembrane domains (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the transmembrane domain analysis, with reference to Figure 4B and source data.

claim: Subpopulations of putative membrane-spanning proteins may potentially serve as candidate hidden antigens that may evade recognition by the host immune system but may be highly accessible to vaccine-induced antibodies.
source: Subpopulations of these putative membrane-spanning proteins may potentially serve as candidate hidden antigens that may evade recognition by the host immune system but may be highly accessible to vaccine-induced antibodies (Munn 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of these proteins, with a citation.

claim: Two expanded subgroups of C2H2-ZF transcription factors are secretory cell specific and lack one-to-one C. elegans orthologs.
source: We generated a phylogeny of B. malayi C2H2-ZF transcription factors and identified two expanded subgroups that are secretory cell specific and that lack one-to-one C. elegans orthologs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis of C2H2-ZF transcription factors, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Several C2H2-ZF transcription factors were also detected in the bulk RNA-seq data of FAC-sorted 'largest' cells.
source: Several of these transcription factors were also detected in the bulk RNA-seq data of FAC-sorted 'largest' cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the FACS-enriched cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Previous studies have reported an enrichment of C2H2-ZF transcription factors in mf-derived ES products and elevated expression of these genes in mf.
source: Previous studies have reported an enrichment of this transcription factor class in mf-derived ES products and elevated expression of these genes in mf (Bennuru et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bennuru et al., 2011 and Choi et al., 2011.

claim: The role of C2H2-ZF proteins in ES cell types is poorly understood, but may involve governing gene regulatory events at the host–parasite interface or to help adapt mf for the stark environmental transition from the mammalian host to the mosquito vector.
source: The role of these proteins in ES cell types is poorly understood, but may involve governing gene regulatory events at the host–parasite interface or to help adapt mf for the stark environmental transition from the mammalian host to the mosquito vector.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of these proteins.

claim: The four β-tubulin B. malayi proteins exhibit broad expression across the mf body, with Bma-btub-1 (Bm4733) most highly expressed compared to all other β-tubulins.
source: The four β-tubulin B. malayi proteins exhibit broad expression across the mf body, with Bma-btub-1 (Bm4733) most highly expressed compared to all other β-tubulins (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the anthelmintic target expression analysis, with reference to Figure 5A and B.

claim: Bma-btub-1 has the highest sequence similarity to the benzimidazole target in C. elegans (ben-1).
source: This β-tubulin also has the highest sequence similarity to the benzimidazole target in C. elegans (ben-1), and we hypothesize that Bma-btub-1 is responsible for mediating the antifilarial action of ABZ.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence similarity analysis.

claim: Bma-btub-1 is hypothesized to be responsible for mediating the antifilarial action of ABZ.
source: This β-tubulin also has the highest sequence similarity to the benzimidazole target in C. elegans (ben-1), and we hypothesize that Bma-btub-1 is responsible for mediating the antifilarial action of ABZ.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on sequence similarity and known drug targets.

claim: Bma-tbb-4 and Bma-mec-7 were minimally represented but found in muscle and neuronal cell types.
source: Bma-tbb-4 and Bma-mec-7 were minimally represented but found in muscle and neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the β-tubulin expression analysis.

claim: The coexpression of β-tubulins in C. elegans cells provides redundancy that allows for normal growth in Cel-ben-1 loss-of-function mutants.
source: The coexpression of β-tubulins in C. elegans cells provides redundancy that allows for normal growth in Cel-ben-1 loss-of-function mutants (Driscoll et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Driscoll et al., 1989.

claim: Single-cell coexpression of β-tubulins within individual B. malayi mf cells shows strong association between Bma-tbb-4 and Bma-btub-1 and a moderate association between Bma-btub-1 and Bma-btub-2.
source: Single-cell coexpression of β-tubulins within individual B. malayi mf cells shows strong association between Bma-tbb-4 and Bma-btub-1 and a moderate association between Bma-btub-1 and Bma-btub-2 (Figure 5C), pointing to potential redundancy and compensatory drug response mechanisms.
evidence: This is a finding from the coexpression analysis, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The coexpression pattern of β-tubulins points to potential redundancy and compensatory drug response mechanisms.
source: Single-cell coexpression of β-tubulins within individual B. malayi mf cells shows strong association between Bma-tbb-4 and Bma-btub-1 and a moderate association between Bma-btub-1 and Bma-btub-2 (Figure 5C), pointing to potential redundancy and compensatory drug response mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coexpression pattern and known biology in C. elegans.

claim: Bma-trp-2 facilitates inward calcium currents upon activation and results in subsequent opening of the SLO-1 K+ channel.
source: Bma-trp-2 facilitates inward calcium currents upon activation and results in subsequent opening of the SLO-1 K+ channel (Verma et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2022), the proposed target of the macrofilaricidal emodepside (Kashyap et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Verma et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2022; and Kashyap et al., 2019.

claim: The majority of Bma-trp-2 and Bma-slo-1 transcripts are found in body wall muscle (clusters 2 and 19).
source: The majority of Bma-trp-2 and Bma-slo-1 transcripts are found in body wall muscle (clusters 2 and 19), consistent with electrophysiological assays (Kashyap et al., 2019; Verma et al., 2020) and the paralytic effect of emodepside.
evidence: This is a finding from the TRP channel expression analysis, with citations supporting the functional relevance.

claim: There is strong evidence that IVM acts on muscle-expressed GluCls adjacent to the secretory apparatus leading to suppression of secretory cargo and host clearance of mf.
source: There is strong evidence that IVM acts on muscle-expressed GluCls adjacent to the secretory apparatus leading to suppression of secretory cargo and host clearance of mf (Harischandra et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014; Loghry et al., 2020; Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The B. malayi GluCl complement (Bma-avr-14, Bma-glc-2, Bma-glc-3, and Bma-glc-4) display expression in neuronal and muscle cell types.
source: The B. malayi GluCl complement (Bma-avr-14, Bma-glc-2, Bma-glc-3, and Bma-glc-4) display expression in neuronal and muscle cell types (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the GluCl expression analysis, with reference to Figure 5A and B.

claim: Bma-avr-14 is noted as an important subunit for IVM sensitivity.
source: Bma-avr-14 is noted as an important subunit for IVM sensitivity (Dent et al., 2000), and the expression of avr-14 in annotated muscle cell types is consistent with its expression in muscle surrounding the ES pore (Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dent et al., 2000 and Moreno et al., 2010.

claim: Not all GluCl subunit compositions are amenable to expression in heterologous systems and it is unclear what channel formations best reflect the native state.
source: While functional B. malayi GluCl channels have been constituted in heterologous systems to determine IVM sensitivity (Choudhary et al., 2022; Lamassiaude et al., 2022), not all subunit compositions are amenable to expression and it is unclear what channel formations best reflect the native state (Lamassiaude et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on heterologous expression of GluCl channels.

claim: Bma-avr-14 and Bma-glc-4 are the most commonly coexpressed GluCl subunits.
source: To improve predictions of native channel compositions, we examined the correlation of GluCl subunit expression in individual cells and identified Bma-avr-14 and Bma-glc-4 as the most commonly coexpressed GluCl subunits (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the GluCl coexpression analysis, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Bma-avr-14 was also coexpressed with Bma-glc-2, a combination reported to be IVM-sensitive.
source: Bma-avr-14 was also coexpressed with Bma-glc-2, a combination reported to be IVM-sensitive; however, Bma-glc-2 was minimally expressed and was not coexpressed with any other GluCl subunit.
evidence: This is a finding from the GluCl coexpression analysis.

claim: The subunits that comprise L-type and P-type nAChR channels are mainly restricted to the body wall muscle.
source: As expected, the subunits that comprise L-type and P-type nAChR channels are mainly restricted to the body wall muscle (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the nAChR expression analysis, with references to figures.

claim: Single-cell coexpression analysis of nAChRs reveals that Bma-acr-15 could be an essential and missing component of our understanding of nAChR composition and function in filarial nematodes.
source: Single-cell coexpression analysis of nAChRs reveals that Bma-acr-15 could be an essential and missing component of our understanding of nAChR composition and function in filarial nematodes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference from the nAChR coexpression analysis, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Cell viability was successfully measured using DRAQ5 (nucleated objects) and Calcein Violet-AM.
source: Cell viability was successfully measured using DRAQ5 (nucleated objects) and Calcein Violet-AM, a shorter wavelength version of the Calcein-AM dye (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a statement of the validation of the viability assay, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Cell health did not decline significantly after dissociation and incubation on ice in media for up to 8 hr.
source: We also confirmed that cell health did not decline significantly after dissociation and incubation on ice in media for up to 8 hr and that DMSO at concentrations required for drug solubility did not compromise cell health (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell viability time course experiment, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: DMSO at concentrations required for drug solubility did not compromise cell health.
source: We also confirmed that cell health did not decline significantly after dissociation and incubation on ice in media for up to 8 hr and that DMSO at concentrations required for drug solubility did not compromise cell health (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the DMSO control experiment, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: We did not observe a significant decrease in cell viability in any of the primary classes of drug at pharmacologically relevant concentrations.
source: We did not observe a significant decrease in cell viability in any of the primary classes of drug at pharmacologically relevant concentrations; however, higher concentrations of IVM did produce a cytotoxic effect (EC50 = 51 ± 5.16 µM) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug dose-response experiments, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Higher concentrations of IVM produced a cytotoxic effect (EC50 = 51 ± 5.16 µM).
source: We did not observe a significant decrease in cell viability in any of the primary classes of drug at pharmacologically relevant concentrations; however, higher concentrations of IVM did produce a cytotoxic effect (EC50 = 51 ± 5.16 µM) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the IVM dose-response experiment, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Muscle, neurons, and unannotated cell types revealed the most significant and abundant upregulation of genes in response to IVM exposure.
source: Compared to the untreated control, muscle, neurons, and unannotated cell types revealed the most significant and abundant upregulation of genes in response to IVM exposure (Figure 6E and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the IVM-treated single-cell RNA-seq analysis, with reference to Figure 6E and source data.

claim: The greatest transcriptional shift occurs in muscle cells, which house the highest transcriptional abundance of GluCls.
source: The greatest transcriptional shift occurs in muscle cells, which house the highest transcriptional abundance of GluCls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the IVM-treated single-cell RNA-seq analysis, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serine protease inhibitor Bma-srp-2 showed the greatest increase in expression in unannotated cluster 8 (Log2FC > 2.8) in response to IVM.
source: Differentially expressed genes of interest include serine protease inhibitor Bma-srp-2, a highly abundant ES product released from mf, which showed the greatest increase in expression in unannotated cluster 8 (Log2FC > 2.8) but was also significantly upregulated in 9 of 27 clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the IVM-treated single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The IVM response was characterized by upregulation of genes previously identified in bulk RNA-seq studies (Bm10661, Bm228, Bm9776, Bma-srp-2, Bm8514, Bma-unc-54.2, Bm33, Bm13260, Bma-rps-28).
source: The IVM response was additionally characterized by upregulation of genes previously identified in bulk RNA-seq studies (Bm10661, Bm228, Bm9776, Bma-srp-2, Bm8514, Bma-unc-54.2, Bm33, Bm13260, Bma-rps-28) (Ballesteros et al., 2016) and proteins with unassigned functions.
evidence: This is a finding from the IVM-treated single-cell RNA-seq analysis, with a citation to a previous bulk RNA-seq study.

claim: Highly viable populations of adhered cells were observed after a 24 hr incubation in 10% FBS L-15 media.
source: Highly viable populations of adhered cells were observed after a 24 hr incubation in 10% FBS L-15 media (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell culture experiment, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: Adhered cells remained viable at 96 hr as indicated by Calcein-AM fluorescence.
source: Adhered cells remained viable at 96 hr as indicated by Calcein-AM fluorescence (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell culture viability time course, with references to figures.

claim: The cultured cells are not actively dividing in the current culture conditions.
source: We assessed the mitotic activity of these cells using an EdU proliferation assay and determined these cells are not actively dividing in the current culture conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the EdU proliferation assay, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The primary action of anthelmintics requires cell–cell connectivity.
source: We directly assessed the effects of anthelmintics on the viability of isolated cells, showing that the major anthelmintic classes do not elicit cell death at pharmacologically relevant concentrations. This suggests that the primary action of these drugs requires cell–cell connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that anthelmintics do not kill isolated cells at pharmacological concentrations.

claim: The action of IVM in C. elegans is innexin-dependent.
source: The action of IVM in C. elegans is innexin-dependent (Dent et al., 2000), underscoring the importance of gap junctions in the signaling cascade that results in the whole-organism drug effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dent et al., 2000.

claim: Exposure of mf to IVM prevents later exsheathment in the mosquito.
source: Exposure of mf to IVM prevents later exsheathment in the mosquito (Rao et al., 1992), which we speculate is consistent with suppression of ES function leading to the trapping of inner-body enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rao et al., 1992, with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The mf ES apparatus is a secretory choke point in the parasite life cycle.
source: This view of the mf ES apparatus as a secretory choke point in the parasite life cycle offers a control target relevant to both the arthropod and mammalian hosts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of the ES apparatus.

claim: Dispersions of embryonic Brugia cells have been performed, but the captured cells do not differentiate in culture.
source: While dispersions of embryonic Brugia cells have been performed, the captured cells do not differentiate in culture (Higazi et al., 2004), limiting the advantages of the system.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Higazi et al., 2004.
